teaching_claim: Pictures, diagrams, paintings, and sculpture are different representational/art forms.
Music/sound can be described using relative perceptual properties.
Earth's day/night cycle and the observable daytime/nighttime sky are related but not identical concepts.
Apparent solar position and shadow change form an observable correlated pattern.
The Moon's visible appearance changes in a recurring pattern over time.
Planets orbit; orbiting is a spatial motion relation.
The solar system contains the Sun and orbiting bodies; member and system are distinct.
Living and nonliving entities are distinguished using biological properties rather than motion alone.
Plants have differentiated structures: roots, stems, leaves, flowers/seeds where applicable.
Plants require resources and pass through growth stages.
Animals can be classified into nested groups using shared features.
Animal structures such as fur, feathers, scales, shells, wings, and fins relate to morphology; movement types are distinct actions.
Habitats are environments in which organisms live; habitat is not synonymous with organism.
Structures can contribute to functions important for survival.
Diet categories concern what organisms eat; feeding relations can form food chains.
Predator and prey describe an ecological interaction, not permanent moral categories.
Animal life cycles include development and reproduction; parent and offspring are distinct individuals.
Offspring can resemble parents while varying from them and from one another.
Organisms in ecosystems can depend on and affect other organisms and environmental resources.
Pollination and seed dispersal are transfer processes that may involve wind, animals, or other mechanisms.
Decomposers contribute to breakdown of dead organic material.
A human body has major external parts organized by part–whole relations.
Sensory systems provide information through vision, hearing, smell, taste, and touch.
Emotions/internal states and externally observable behavior are related but not identical.
Symptoms are experienced/reported states that can motivate health-related action without themselves uniquely determining a diagnosis.
Body systems are decomposed into interacting subsystems rather than taught as one C123 mega-lesson.
Support/movement and breathing are distinct body functions with interacting structures.
Circulation transports materials through the body.
Digestion transforms and moves food through an ordered process.
Brain/nerves participate in receiving and coordinating information.
Germs can contribute to illness; prevention reduces risk but does not imply certainty.
Persistent named agents. A name can continue to refer to the same individual across lessons; L000 establishes Ninereeds, Taro, Emma, Bob, Errol and their acquaintance with Ninereeds.
Rules, laws, advice, permission, prohibition, rights, and responsibilities are distinct normative relations.
Governments/leaders perform responsibilities and collective functions; details vary by polity.
Groups can make collective choices using procedures such as voting.
Sender–message–receiver. Communication can involve a sender, transferable message, and receiver.
Communication media include phone, email, radio, and other channels; channel and message are distinct.
Computing systems can receive inputs and produce outputs.
Files, records, and data can be stored; storage location and represented information are distinct.
A network contains connected nodes and links over which information may move.
Paths, addresses, routing, local/distant connections, and failures are distinct network concepts.
The Internet is a networked system rather than a single device or single location.
Looking for information and successfully finding it are different events.
An algorithm is an ordered procedure that may include conditional branches.
Programs contain instructions interpreted/executed by computing systems.
Debugging is systematic diagnosis/revision after observed failure or error.
Automation allows a system to perform assigned operations without a person manually doing every step.
Customs and traditions vary across groups and are not universal human rules.
Languages and writing systems are conventional symbolic systems and can differ.
Beliefs/worldviews are attributed to people or traditions; differing beliefs can be represented without curricular endorsement.
Celebrations/ceremonies have culturally situated purposes and forms.
Tables and charts are representations of data, not the measured entities themselves.
Trends describe changes/relationships across data rather than individual observations.
Weather is a state of atmospheric conditions that can be described and measured.
Weather patterns and seasons concern recurrence over time, not guarantees about individual days.
Water-cycle processes are distinct transformations/movements that can form a cycle.
Natural resources have sources and uses; waste, reuse, recycling, and conservation are distinct responses.
Atmosphere, water, land, and living systems interact.
Price and money quantify exchange value in a transaction.
Sufficiency: available quantity/resources may or may not meet a requirement.
Goods and services distinguish produced/provided things from activities.
Jobs connect roles, workplaces, employers/organizations, and activities.
Production can occur through farms, factories, workshops, and service systems.
Supply chains connect stages of production, movement, and provision.
Buying/selling, saving/spending, scarcity, and trade are distinct exchange/resource relations.
Machines/systems consist of interacting parts; part failure can affect system behavior.
Engineering proceeds through problem/requirement → proposed solution → test → observed result → revision.
Knowledge and ignorance. An agent may know something, not know it, or ask another agent who may know.
Belief correction. An earlier belief or statement can be wrong and later corrected without changing the speaker's identity.
Source vs content. Who supplied a statement and what the statement says are different pieces of information.
Observation vs inference. What is directly observed is distinct from a conclusion drawn from observations plus prior knowledge.
Books, reports, news, and references are information sources with provenance.
Fact, opinion, knowledge, belief, and preference are overlapping but nonidentical epistemic categories.
Claims may be supported by evidence; evidence has sources and may support claims to differing degrees.
Uncertainty admits degrees; prediction is not certainty.
Definitions specify intended meanings; definitions and examples perform different functions.
Classification organizes entities by shared criteria; category membership may be nested.
Similarity and difference depend on the property or criterion being compared.
Memory is stored/retrieved information about prior experience and can differ from current observation.
Action, state, and routine. Something happening now differs from a recurring routine or relatively stable state.
Procedure. A task can consist of ordered steps where sequence may affect the result.

Routes and paths. Travel can have a start, path, intermediate places, and destination. In the canonical world, the Meadow Path connects Gran's garden gate to the Pond and continues to the School; the Pond is a short walk from the Oak.
Landforms such as mountains, valleys, plains, and coasts are distinguishable geographic structures.
Rivers, lakes, and oceans differ; flowing water can move from source through a path into a larger body.
Cardinal directions support relative geographic orientation.
Addresses and geographic hierarchies locate entities at multiple scales.
A hazard is a condition/event with potential for harm; hazard, damage, and response are distinct.
Fire/heat and dangerous-material hazards have warning, avoidance, and response concepts.
Severe weather, flooding, and geologic hazards require condition-specific responses rather than one generic script.
Everyday practices and technologies can differ between past and present.
Change can accumulate across generations while some continuities remain.
Stories have characters, settings, events, and ordered sequences.
Narrated dialogue and reported speech represent conversational events.
Fiction/nonfiction is a relation between text and intended representation/claims, not simply “interesting vs boring.”
Objects can be composed of materials; material and finished object are distinct.
Materials differ in observable/measurable properties such as hardness, texture, and flexibility.
Solid, liquid, and gas are distinguishable states of matter at an introductory level.
Heating/cooling can accompany changes of state or form; process and resulting state are distinct.
Quantity and zero. Finite collections can have quantities, including no members. Exact initial numerical ceiling is UNSPECIFIED.
Compare quantities. Two collections can contain more, fewer, or equal numbers of members.
Addition: combining collections changes total quantity.
Subtraction: removing members changes the remaining quantity.
Distribution and equal shares: objects can be allocated across recipients.
Ordinal position: quantity and position-in-order are different.
Two-dimensional shapes and attributes.
Three-dimensional forms, faces, edges, and other attributes.
Measurement compares a property with a unit; length, height, and width are distinct dimensions.
Mass and capacity are distinct measurable properties.
Whole and fractional parts such as half and quarter.
Repeating patterns have identifiable units and continuation rules.
Training examples/data provide observations from which a learning system can derive useful regularities.
Features/patterns and predictions are distinct: observed inputs support but do not guarantee predictions.
Training, testing, error, and generalization are different stages/relations; performance on examples does not establish universal correctness.
Ordinary physical objects and persistence. Objects can remain the same object while their location or visible state changes.
Ownership/belonging. An object can belong to a person or other recognized owner; owner and object are distinct.
Properties vs identity. Color, size, and shape are properties of an object; changing a property description does not automatically create a new object.
Mind/person/device distinctions. Minds, people, and devices are not interchangeable categories; Ninereeds and Errol are curricular instances of minds.

teaching_claim: Mind transfer vs message transfer. Errol may travel by data transfer; a message may travel without Errol traveling. These are distinct events.
Copying data and moving data are different operations; sameness of information need not imply sameness of physical instance.
Interface or device replacement need not by itself define identity or continuity; metaphysical conclusions remain explicitly out of scope.
Pushes, pulls, and motion. Interactions such as pushes and pulls can start, stop, or change observable motion.
Speed compares rates of motion.
Simple machines alter how forces are applied; decomposed by lever/pulley/inclined-plane examples rather than one vocabulary dump.
Magnets interact with some materials and not others.
Light enables ordinary visual perception of objects; sources, paths, and objects are distinct.
Shadows arise when light paths are blocked; shadow and object are not identical.
Sound and vibration are causally related in simple observable systems.
A simple circuit contains connected components whose arrangement affects operation.
Energy sources supply energy to processes/systems at an introductory descriptive level.
Need vs want. Needing something and preferring/wanting it are different relations.
Agents can act toward goals for reasons/motives.
Appropriate expression can vary by partner, setting, purpose, and degree of formality.
Representation vs referent. An icon or picture may represent Errol without being Errol.

Maps as representations of places. A map is not the place itself; marks and symbols can represent locations and routes. The School is at the far end of the Meadow Path, and the supplied world-bible topology is authoritative.
Signs, icons, labels, and symbols use representational conventions.
Scientific/computational models are simplified representations whose omissions and purposes matter.
Authentication/access/privacy concern who is allowed to access information or systems.
Known vs unknown person. A person may be known to one participant and unknown to another; introducing someone changes that relation.
Communication breakdown. A hearer/reader may fail to understand even when a message was produced; participants can notice the failure.
Cooperation. Multiple agents can share a goal and perform complementary actions or help one another.
Disagreement and conflict. Agents can disagree about facts, preferences, or plans without being different identities or necessarily being enemies.
Promise/commitment. A promise connects a speaker now with an intended later action.
Trust and reliability. Expectations about another agent may be influenced by whether prior commitments or claims proved reliable; trust is not certainty.
Fairness. Fairness concerns how rules, turns, resources, or reasons apply to participants; it is not reducible in every case to identical outcomes.
Households and family relationships are social relations, not assumptions about universal household structure.
Clubs, teams, organizations, and other groups have membership relations.
Occupations describe roles/work people perform; person and occupation are distinct.
Public services perform functions for communities.
Institutions such as schools, libraries, clinics, and banks are organized social places/functions.
Objects/systems can contain parts; part, whole, member, material, and component relations must not be conflated.
Communication device. Errol communicates through Gran's phone; the phone is an ordinary device and is not Errol.
Tools and designed functions. A tool is an object used to perform an action or purpose; the tool is distinct from the user and result.
Clocks, dates, calendars, and conventional temporal coordinates.
Before/after and duration order events without collapsing them into one tense.
Yesterday/today/tomorrow are deictic time frames; past and future are taught separately rather than as C071's three-way bundle.
Age and generations relate individuals to elapsed time without defining identity.
Physical transportation. People can change physical location using different means; Emma may travel by bus and Taro by bicycle.
